title: Software Supply Chain Assurance
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Software Supply Chain Assurance.
Apply software supply chain assurance to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers software supply chain assurance in the DevSecOps and Software Supply Chain Security track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Protect pipeline identities and artifacts, pin and review dependencies, keep secrets out of logs, and require human approval for high-impact changes. The specific focus here is software supply chain assurance; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Software Supply Chain Assurance focuses on supplier and dependency risk; build provenance; artifact signing and verification. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Supplier and Dependency Risk
items.text: Cloud and delivery security combine least-privilege identities, hardened defaults, approved dependencies, secret management, artifact provenance, logging, and repeatable deployment checks. Verify service-specific behavior and avoid placing secrets in source or logs.

items.title: Build Provenance
items.text: For build provenance, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Artifact Signing and Verification
items.text: For artifact signing and verification, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Reproducible Builds
items.text: For reproducible builds, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Software Composition Analysis
items.text: Describe the endpoints, addressing, protocol, direction, and expected behavior before diagnosing a network issue. Use read-only commands, authorized packet captures, and synthetic examples; do not infer compromise from one unusual packet alone.

items.title: Secure Release Management
items.text: For secure release management, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Supply Chain Incident Response
items.text: Incident response follows the current organizational plan and coordinates analysis, containment, recovery, communication, and improvement. Preserve needed evidence, document decisions, and escalate actions that may disrupt business or safety.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: DevSecOps makes security verifiable throughout build, review, release, deployment, and maintenance instead of leaving it until the end. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Software Supply Chain Assurance focuses on supplier and dependency risk; build provenance; artifact signing and verification. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Software Supply Chain Assurance. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Supplier and Dependency Risk; Build Provenance; Artifact Signing and Verification), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.
content.expected_output:
dependency_check: True
secret_scan: True
untrusted_pull_request_write_access: False
manual_release_approval: True
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Software Supply Chain Assurance is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.
